physical_harm: Injuries and harm caused to the seven-year-old girl, including discharge on her private parts and stomach
number_of_offences: Charged under Section 376(2)(f) and 511 IPC; upheld under Section 376(2)(f) and 511 IPC
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the prosecution's evidence that the accused raped a seven-year-old girl, including the prosecutrix's testimony, her mother's account, and medical evidence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that the trial court had properly evaluated their testimony and that the High Court had failed to consider the contradictions in the prosecution's evidence.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 27.12.2008; Trial judgment: 01.02.2010; High Court decision: 01.02.2010; Supreme Court decision: JULY01, 2015
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: DIPAK MISRA, J. and Asha Jain Madan; Counsel for the State: G.D. Singh, Apoorv Kurup, Shreya Dubey
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Section 376(2)(f) IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for five years; High Court: Converted the offence to one under Section 354 IPC and confined the sentence to the period of custody already undergone; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, remitted the matter back to the High Court for a fresh decision
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused raped a seven-year-old girl and that the conviction under Section 376(2)(f) read with Section 511 of the Indian Penal Code was valid, with the accused sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for five years.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court had improperly converted the offence to one under Section 354 IPC and reduced the sentence to the period already undergone, citing a compromise between the accused and the parents of the victim.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that in cases of rape or attempted rape, there cannot be a compromise or settlement as it would be against the honour of the victim, which is sacrosanct. The Court emphasized that the appellate court must reappreciate the evidence and not dismiss appeals summarily without examining the evidence.
precedent_relied_upon: Amar Singh v. Bawinder Singh and Others 2003 (1) SCR 754 : (2003) 2 SCC 518; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhura Kunjda (2009) 17 SCC 346; Shimbhu and Another v. State of Haryana 2013 (14) SCR 136 : (2014) 13 SCC 318; Shyam Narain v. State (NCT of Delhi) 2013 (8) SCR 951 : (2013) 7 SCC 77; Baldev Singh v. State of Punjab 2011 (15) SCR 927 : (2011) 13 SCC 705; Ravindra v. State of Madhya Pradesh 2015 (2) SCR 860: (2015) 4 SCC 491
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed as the High Court had improperly converted the offence to one under Section 354 IPC and reduced the sentence to the period already undergone, which the Supreme Court found to be against the legal principles and the dignity of the victim.
other_sentence_order: The matter was remitted back to the High Court for a fresh decision, and the respondent was to be taken into custody forthwith by the concerned Superintendent of Police.
